en: The Liturgy of Praise for the National Teacher Qingliang of the Avataṃsaka (with Preface), composed by Chángshuì Zhìgēng, a Dharma descendant.

Our ancestor, the National Teacher Xuánshǒu, established the school and categorized the teachings. He exhausted the entirety of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* across its generations and severed the arguments of the hundred schools. In his exegesis...

During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, the translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* reached its nineteenth fascicle when, before his great vow was fulfilled, [Fazang] suddenly passed away into true quiescence.
When Cōngláng (Chengguan) first ascended the Dharma seat of Xuánshǒu, he studied and transmitted the meanings of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and other texts.

Realizing that there is no fixed teacher for one’s studies, he traveled to the north to inquire about the Li school and to the south to seek out the Fa school. Carrying his book-cases, he journeyed through the four quarters, traversing the three vehicles of study, and subsequently proceeded further.

The worthy master Jiangsha had recently passed away. Although his disciples—such as the eminent leaders of the school, Huiyuan and Huiying—continued his unfinished drafts, none of them adhered to the traditions of the ancients. Thus, Qingliang suddenly gave vent to a sigh of lamentation.

Therefore, he separately composed a new commentary on the sutra in twenty fascicles (alternatively expanded to forty fascicles), and a *Suíjīng yǎnyì chāo* (Explanatory Notes Following the Sutra) in forty fascicles (alternatively expanded to sixty or eighty fascicles).
Both this commentary and the notes do not deviate from the intention of the former master. Among the disciples of Xianshou, they were as numerous as the stars;

among them, those with white eyebrows and blue eyes stood out as the most eminent, transcending their peers. Their realization of the Way accorded with the conditions, and they transmitted the teachings through mind-to-mind communion and oral instruction. They alone...
The *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Dà Sòng Gāosēng Zhuàn*), within the section on Exegesis (*Yìjiě kē*), at the end of the biography of Master Zàng, states:

"The single school of Huayan was transmitted to Chengguan (the National Teacher’s posthumous name). Furthermore, this master composed the *Suíwén Shòujiàn* (Hand Mirror Following the Text) in one hundred fascicles.

*Huayan Gangyao* (Essentials of the Avataṃsaka) in three fascicles; *Fajie Xuanjing* (Mysterious Mirror of the Dharma Realm) in one fascicle; *Jingdeng Shuowen* (Explanations of the Text on the Lamp-Mirror) in one fascicle;

*Sansheng Yuanrong Guan* (Contemplation on the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages) in one fascicle; more than thirty works concerning the essential connections of the sūtras and vinayas, such as the *Huayan Yuanjue Si-fen Zhongguan* (The Middle Contemplation of the Four Sections of the Avataṃsaka’s Perfect Enlightenment);

the *Huayan Qiuchu Jiuhui Huazangjie Tu* (Diagram of the Flower Treasury World of the Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies of the Avataṃsaka); *Xinjing Shuowen* (Explanations of the Text on the Mind-Mirror) in one fascicle; and the *Dajing* (Great Sūtra).

The *Liaoyi beiyao* (Essential Compendium of Definitive Meaning) in three fascicles contains the texts of the lectures delivered by the Imperial Preceptor of the Tang dynasty before the Emperor at dawn, as well as the ancestral teachings of his own school, including poems, memorials, and official correspondence, totaling over eighty fascicles.
Minister Pei remarked: "Ancient brocade and pure gold are employed according to their respective vessels;

it is truly because he imparts the Dharma according to the capacity of the recipient that the ocean responds with its many waves. Though the profound meanings and elegant discourses differ, they ultimately converge upon a single principle. Throughout [his career]...
He served as the gatekeeper and teacher to seven emperors during nine successive reigns. His secular lifespan was one hundred and eight years, and his monastic seniority reached eighty-three years.
His stature was nine feet and four inches tall; with his hands hanging down, they reached below his knees. His eyes emitted light at night and remained without blinking during the day.

His discourse was refined and elegant, and his conduct served as a model for others. He possessed the skill to hold two writing brushes simultaneously; the works he authored that have survived and been transmitted amount to over four hundred fascicles.

(As stated above... Because the status of the National Preceptor was lofty and profound, and his understanding and practice were subtle and deep, he upheld the Great Teaching with might and illuminated the grand tradition with the lamp of wisdom.
Even among those who possessed vast, profound, and subtle learning and completed the words of the Buddha for a single generation, after Xianshou, it was my Master who inherited [the lineage];
thus, the merit belongs to Qingliang. Every year in the middle month of winter, all quarters universally observe this as the anniversary of Xianshou’s passing, focusing exclusively on...

I have offered praise and offerings; the various patriarchs are merely listed in succession. Alas! To attribute merit to the ancestral virtues of Qingliang, one ought to perform a dedicated sacrifice.

Recently, I obtained the original biographies of the two Dharma Masters, Zongmi and Sengrui, from Ou-yue. Their divine spirits stand in reverent attendance at the incense table. Their icy countenances are lofty and bright, their majestic spirit transcendent;
they appear as if still present in all their dignity. Those who behold them feel both awe and love. I specifically seek this for the long-term benefit of the assembly.

The artisan has transcribed this. It being the dawn of the sixth day of the third month, I have briefly presented these meager offerings. As there are many fellow students here, they all requested of me, saying:
"While the sumptuous array of delicacies is complete, we lack verses of praise. We pray that you will compose a literary work, so as to honor the ancient models.

Thereupon, disregarding my own dullness and ignorance, I have briefly offered these hymns of praise, following the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and inheriting the phrases and sentences of Qingliang (Chengguan).

To trace back their merits and aspire to their grace, and to diligently perform sacrifices and offerings—is this not indeed appropriate? As for the reason each position uses "Yilong" (Dragon of Meaning) as its title:
when Xianshou first met Master Yunhua Yan, he was able to pose several questions that all transcended the master's expectations. Master Yan sighed and said:
"Among those who have come here, even those like Yilong rarely inquire into such matters; how much more so, then, for you, a virtuous and wise one, to have illuminated my ears and eyes! Furthermore—
The eminent monk Huìróng made this vow: "If I do not become known as the 'Dragon of Meaning' after thirty years of study, I shall never return home.
Later, his fame indeed resounded far and wide. Furthermore, regarding the *Huayan Sūtra Commentary* composed at Mount Wutai, Qingliang, it is said that he dreamed his body became a dragon;

its head rested upon the Southern Terrace while its tail coiled around the Northern Terrace, and it departed emitting light in many directions—a propitious omen for the widespread circulation of the text. Moreover...

Pei, the State Councilor, respectfully received the imperial decree to compose the inscription for the *Qīngliáng Miàojiào Tǎ* (Stupa of the Sublime Enlightenment of Qingliang). The inscription reads: By imperial command, his likeness was to be depicted; yet the characteristic of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself markless.
A great dragon of the Sea-Seal (*sāgaramudrā*), he dwells coiled within the *fangzhàng* (abbot’s quarters). Now, he is referred to as "Yilong" (Dragon of Meaning) for this very reason.
If one examines the Bodhisattva of Qingliang, his meritorious virtues are inconceivable; how could Yilong alone suffice? For those at the beginning of their studies, there should be no doubt.
(The practitioner enters the ritual arena, spreads the mat, performs three prostrations, kneels with the right knee on the ground, holds the incense burner, and chants:

"Respectfully, [I acknowledge] the wondrous arts that penetrate all quarters and the profound regulations that have prevailed from time immemorial. These are constantly proclaimed throughout the seven locations and nine assemblies, fully endowed with the six..."
The ten mysteries of the marks are extensively expounded; the waves of the ocean of meaning are vast and boundless. First, the supreme melody soars high;

second, the purport of the teachings is perfectly integrated, beyond the hearing of those of the Two Vehicles. Without shifting even a single hair’s breadth, it horizontally encompasses the entire Dharma-realm;

without moving for a single kṣaṇa, it vertically penetrates through the long duration of time. It exhausts the great source of nature and characteristics and reaches the level path of fruit and cause, transcending all.

As for its principles, they surpass lofty peaks; as it encompasses the various sutras, it is like rivers flowing into the vast deep. It brightens the golden sun, eclipsing the light of all other luminaries;
it clarifies the jade hare, obscuring the splendor of the remaining stars. Its profundity is beyond measure; its mysteries are inconceivable.

It is not that those of lower realms can know it; only those of superior faculties may enter it. Thus, from the Dragon Palace the wondrous was selected and at the Phoenix Gate the numinous was translated.
The *Avataṃsaka* blossomed profusely in West India, its full leaves and fragrance spreading throughout the Eastern Land. It is a teaching that imparts instruction without partiality.
The Five Heavens welcomed the grace of the True Wind, which spread far and wide without obstruction; the myriad nations were moistened by the rain of the Dharma.

Throughout the ages, there have never been a lack of masters and their disciples who possessed perfect enlightenment; among both sages and ordinary beings, those who responded to this inspiration have appeared anew for later generations of scholars.
Xianshou first sang the "Snowy Hymn," and Qingliang followed with the "Vernal Spring. Fazhao and Fazang elucidated the paths of the five teachings and embodied the Great Dharma, guiding [all beings].
The path of the ten schools manifested its form within the lineage of Yu and descended its traces during the Tang dynasty.

Admiring the fragrance of the *campaka* among the flowers and envying the nobility of the *candana* within the forest, he shaved off his beard and hair and cast aside his robes and pins. Vastly, he departed from the home of the three realms;
expansively, he awakened from the dream of the four modes of birth. With eloquence granted by heaven and knowledge innate through study, he served as [the preceptor] for seven emperors.
The Gate-Master traversed the sagely eras of the nine schools; his virtue was like dense, gathering clouds, and his fame spread like fluttering wings.

He stood as a solitary beacon among the monastic community and walked alone at the head of the ranks of monks. Now that his transformative influence has ceased, it is a spring when flowers wither and willows shed their leaves;

his great tasks are complete, marking a season where only the warbling of orioles and the arrival of swallows remain. On this anniversary of his passing, a simple ritual offering is appropriately presented.
With these words in the vernacular, I humbly present this offering of water and herbs to slightly recompense the Dharma-milk and minutely repay your vast kindness.

I pray that your Dharma-eye may see clearly through all things and that your other-mind may be manifest and responsive. May the resonance between teacher and disciple be like the moon reflected in water;
may you behold my sincere devotion and deign to descend and appear before me.
(Perform one prostration, rise, kneel with alternating knees,
and hold the incense burner while inviting:
With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou, the Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Qingliang.
(Three requests and three prostrations, followed by the recitation of the verse:
I bow my head to the ocean of Bodhisattvas of the Avataṃsaka, Whose minds have long cultivated the compassionate vows of Samantabhadra;
To those who rely on the wondrous penetration of the four reliances, And whose meritorious cultivation of the fifth stage has reached the ground difficult to surpass.
Having deeply transcended liberation through the three contemplations, you were about to realize the perfect fusion of the ten bodies.
Manifesting partial forms to transform beings, you resided in the Tang Dynasty; your preaching of the Dharma universally moistened those born within the lineage of Yu.
Your voice shook the world, serving as a model for all, and your fame reached beyond the realm, such that everyone revered you as a master.
Born between the Dragon, the Vinaya-master, and the Tiger, the State Preceptor and Head of the Sangha, Tanuo, is a rare portent.
(At this point, present the written petition;
otherwise, compose a memorial and proclaim it.)
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning Xianshou, the Venerable Qingliang,
whose body was refreshed at the time of his birth from the womb (combining the character "Qingliang" with it).

The Four Reliances took birth in the royal lineage; Ten months of gestation produced the holy embryo, a rare and wondrous omen that moved the hearts of the masses. A brilliant radiance startled the neighboring houses;
with star-like eyes illuminating the world, he was cradled in swaddling clothes. With a torrential eloquence like the ocean, he was wrapped in robes and quilts.
Because the nature of Sudhana is naturally that of a youthful seeker (*kumārabhūta*), and he once again opens the precious treasury of innate virtues,
I single-mindedly take refuge in and pay homage to him (the following sections are to be modeled after this).

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning that is Xianshou, and to the Venerable Qingliang— who, as a playful youth entering the monastery,
fashioned a stupa image with sand and mud, his merit equaling that of a hundred youths, as he frolicked amidst the assembly of various arts.
Heeding the call, he rode his white horse to the green mountains; Delighting in the Jewel Grove, he crossed over cloud-covered ridges.
Sweeping away the six dusts to seek liberation, He ascended the four wisdoms to study Bodhi.
Within one circuit of the stellar year, his spiritual faculties were awakened; The subtle words of the Tripiṭaka, he understood them all.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou; to the Venerable Qingliang, who received the imperial grace of tonsure.
Having shaved his head and donned the black robes, he cast off worldly airs; by following the prohibitions under imperial grace, he entered the ranks of the Sangha.
Golden scissors cut through the drifting green silk; The jade seal shines brightly as the imperial yellow edict settles it.
The stūpa’s blessings transcend and its merit is profound; The hair on the crown is completely free from dust and defilement.
Form is provisional while the mind is truly wondrous and inconceivable— This is indeed the Cloud of Virtue arising from samādhi.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou, who is the ocean of the Avataṃsaka teachings; to the Venerable Qingliang, the temporal embodiment who expounded the commentaries on the various sutras;
and to those who refined the means of expression, roamed upon the blade of wisdom, composed the sections with ease, and sharpened the point of their eloquence.
The *Śūraṅgama* and *Samantabhadra* penetrate the expressive words; the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa* clarify that which is understood.
With a jade hook suspended from the heart of the brocade river, he casts a golden lure into the waves of doctrinal flowers.
In the great surges, his original intent is to seize the whales and turtles; fourteen light nets are skillfully set as expedient means.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dragon of Meaning from the Sea of Avataṃsaka Teachings, Xianshou; and to the Venerable Qingliang, the timely embodiment who precisely transmitted the various treatises.
In their exegesis and investigation of the school’s tenets, they all upheld their resolve, delving deeply into the study of wisdom without following their own subjective minds.
Ten cities were bestowed as rewards for his brilliance; at the window of the dim lamp, he was renowned in five days. He excelled at the snow-covered desk;
having received personal instructions on Yoga from Master Qixin, he inherited the lineage of the *Abhidharmakośa*, *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha*, and *Madhyāntavibhāga*.

Through the power of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and *Ratnagotravibhāga*, he roared like a lion amidst the nine treatises, his arguments bold and formidable. His rigorous assistance in discussing the "Four Excellences" with Master Zhaogong was truly peerless.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou, who is the ocean of the Avataṃsaka teachings; to the Venerable Qingliang, who dwells at ease contemplating the Dharma-body;
who guides others toward the Great Vehicle and peers into the Buddha-eye; whose conduct is as pure and still as a deep pool, and whose meditative mind is far-reaching.
Leaving behind worldly attachments, one wanders through the contemplation of the lotus; Within the dharma-realm, form and emptiness vanish as they merge.
Upon Mount Tai, the ground of wisdom shines with clarity; On Mount Zhong, the stages of the mind appear distinctly.
Returning to the source, profound stillness washes away worldly toil; Suddenly, one realizes the principle of universal radiance and equality.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dragon of Meaning from the Flower Ornament’s ocean of teachings, the Venerable Qingliang, who was the embodiment of the perfect and luminous precepts;
may all those who aspire to the stage of *pudgala* attain Buddhahood, and may they bestow the merit of their purified ethical discipline upon all living beings.
The tracks of the Śrāvakas exhaustively investigate the limits; The chariot of the Bodhisattva holds the heavy reins and governs the laws of what is permitted and prohibited.
In the uniquely wondrous place where awakening unfolds, the precepts ascend to the highest tier of the pavilion.
The ten great vows are as firm as a life-preserving bag; the three clusters of pure conduct are like a precious mirror reflecting beauty and ugliness.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning that is Xianshou; to the Nameless Master who bears witness, the Venerable Qingliang, embodiment of the timely body.
The Dharma-realm is profoundly still, transcending words and traces; the School of the Lineage is free from conceptual thought, transmitted mind-to-mind.
The Teachings exhaust the source and reach the branches; Chan awakens one to the profound depths and penetrates the very marrow.
Through silent contemplation, one realizes the interest in emptiness and stillness; as a nameless exemplar, one seeks beyond names.
Clearly illuminating both speech and silence as they melt into one—how can this be compared to the futile exhaustion of counting grains of sand?

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou, who is the ocean of the Avataṃsaka teachings; to the Venerable Qingliang, the temporal embodiment who can expound the sutras upon hearing them.
All marvel that the mind of *nirvāṇa* is easy to understand, yet who can awaken to the fact that the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify?
Without mounting the great causal wheel of perfection, How could one reach the vast ocean of the true fruit?
The inexhaustible point of return is seen upon the palm; Inconceivable dharmic arts are sealed within the breast.
With a second cycle, you can expound moving words; The grand regulations of the Dharma-realm now rest with you.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou; to the Venerable Qingliang, the embodiment of the Five Peaks during the era of invocation;
may the Sage’s wisdom grant secret empowerment for the *Ratnakūṭa*, and may the majestic power and strength of the Dragon Honored One be bestowed upon me.
For ten years, the phoenix-brush has threaded through the heart of the blossoms; Upon five-layered phoenix-stationed paper, the moon-like aspirations are inscribed.
True companions earnestly requested the exposition of the newly established meaning; The Dharma Master opened up and expanded upon the new text.
The red-bearded and white-footed ones both propagated the Truth; Like pouring from one vessel into another, clouds arise in response—this is a fitting metaphor.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Master Xianshou, the Dragon of Meaning, who taught the Avataṃsaka; to the Venerable Qingliang, who mastered both Confucianism and Buddhism and served as a bridge between the ages.
Though secular learning offers no benefit, it is a Buddhist injunction that the convergence of Daoism and Confucianism with Buddhism is the beginning of universal understanding.
I take the Five Teachings as my fundamental practice to serve as a balance, And grasp the Nine Classics together as the Red Dipper.
The *Daodejing* and *Zhuangzi* are the aspirations of Xuyao; The *Odes*, *Documents*, benevolence, and righteousness are the hearts of Kong and Yan.
The four surrounding classics and their commentaries are the core of the Five Sciences; The Ten Wings and the hundred schools are all studied with focused attention.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou. When the Commentary was completed, the Venerable Qingliang appeared in a dream;
his Dharma-food and celebratory prose were like a phoenix giving birth to its young, while the auspicious omen of the transmission of fragrance was fulfilled as he became a dragon in a dream.
The radiant scales and fins span the two terraces; His world-illuminating brilliance surpasses the bright sun.
With vigorous strides he manifests transformations as clear as a shuttle; He parts like a thunderbolt-sword, a prophecy for its circulation.
As the hundred rivers enter the sea, their flavors become uniformly salty; In his skill with brocade and blade, his achievement is no small matter.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Dragon of Meaning from Xianshou, who is the ocean of the Avataṃsaka teachings; to the Venerable Qingliang, the temporal embodiment who universally transformed others through his commentaries on the sutras.
Five-colored clouds coalesce as auspicious omens in the heavens; people from the eight directions throng around the Immortal upon earth.
Joy overflows throughout the Nine Provinces as the breeze of compassion fans out; The Dharma rain flies afar across the Four Seas, moistening all.
At the crimson curtains, the pine-needle whisk transmits the teachings to hundreds; In the lecture hall, the staff of discourse inspires thousands of disciples.
The great masters of the famous academies all don the pivotal robes; They hasten toward you, risking their lives, seeking your medicine to heal them.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning that is Xianshou; to the assembly of eminent scholars who composed various commentaries, and to the Venerable Qingliang, the temporal embodiment of the Dharma;
to those who recorded the meanings and composed the texts for the benefit of the Prime Minister; and to the Duke of Hui, whose brush produced exquisite elegance for the sake of the high officials.
The seven noble families store pearls and treasures in their chests; the ten famous monasteries keep brocades and silks in their bags.
The two essentials, the five chapters, and the contemplations of the Three Holy Ones; the various barriers, the double mirrors, and the diagrams of the Nine Classics.
These are the merits of the entangled roots and towering trunk of the manifold flowers; the power of the spreading leaves and hanging shade lies in the force of the chapters and verses.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning that is Xianshou; to the Venerable Qingliang, who manifested in this age to compose the *Hymn on the Translation of the New Sūtra*;
and to the Sage Rui of Uḍḍiyāna, who enhanced its wondrous principles—may you all have joined me in the translation hall as co-translators.
In lecturing and praising, why trouble yourself with dreams and easy words? To propagate the Dharma, one need not rely on immortal incantations.
Flowers bloom in layers upon layers of brocade; Clouds rise across the vast sky, each fragment new.
With lofty discourse on the Holy Dharma, you awaken the Emperor’s mind; The National Preceptor further bestows upon you the title "Qingliang" (Cool and Refreshing).

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou; to the Venerable Qingliang, who encountered the True Dharma in person during his time;
whose longevity was equal to that of the Nine Sovereigns, and whose virtue was as lofty as that of the Kings of the Seven Dynasties.
Outstanding figures from the four quarters pay homage to the Master; The refined elites of the Three Teachings acclaim him as the Head Seat.
Like sunflowers and morning glories, hearts incline toward his light amidst worldly truths; As the day declines like the setting sun, he unfolds the sublime Way.
His poems and memorials move the august imperial court; Discussing the sutras before the Emperor, they rejoice in this auspicious assembly.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Teachings, the Dragon of Meaning, Xianshou; to the Venerable Qingliang, who withdrew his light and entered parinirvāṇa.
When his conditions were exhausted, the four minds perished together; he withdrew his light for three months to manifest impermanence.
The high ministers wore white silk, their hearts grieving for the worthy one; the Emperor suspended court, his sacred mind filled with sorrow.
The stone chamber and burial niche received the honors of the state; the clay statues erected in Tang moved the celestial bodies.
At the cremation, the tongue remained firm like a red lotus; thousands of śarīras shone with lustrous colors.
(At this point, kneel again, hold the incense burner, and visualize while reciting the Five Repentances.

For the sake of the four debts of gratitude and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm of the three realms of existence, I vow that they shall all sever the three obstacles; I take refuge and repent.
(Alternatively, one may employ the ten minds of direct and reverse order, which is not at variance with principle.
With a sincere heart, I repent;
having suddenly forgotten the vast nature of Vairocana, I have leaped recklessly into the shoreless ocean of suffering.
The waves and ripples of the thousand flowers are fundamentally the Buddha-mind; The bubbles that form the five aggregates are the marks of sentient beings.
The wondrous excellence of the ten bodies is confined within the shell of a physical form; The radiance of the ten wisdoms falls into the delusions of emotion.
If one dharma is slightly lost, all dharmas are lost; If a single speck of dust momentarily arises, all specks of dust arise.
Sudden differences in the three virtues result in the three poisons; how could one realize that the ordinary mind is itself the sacred mind?
The constant light of the ten lands is not seen by the blind; though it is preached everywhere throughout the ten directions, the deaf hear nothing.
Though they have ascended to the Vinaya, they are like mad elephants; having fallen under the sway of Māra, they are like mute sheep.
The six marks are entirely deficient, dimming the lamp of clear wisdom; The ten mysteries are perpetually lacking, failing the hanging bright mirror.
Through a hundred negations and four propositions, light slander increases; Throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, heavy transgressions are bound.
My essence is the gate of wisdom through the contemplation of true emptiness; In the perfect fusion of cultivation and nature, I perform this complete repentance.
Having finished the repentance, take refuge with a sincere heart in the Triple Gem (the following sections shall follow this pattern).
With a sincere heart,
I exhort [the Buddhas] to dwell within the space of a single pore— vast as the atoms of a microdust— and to preach the sutras throughout oceans of kalpas in every instant.
Within the mirror-light Indra-net assembly hall, may the wheel of Dharma be turned until the end of time;
with a sincere heart,
I rejoice in the myriad roots of goodness perfected through the eight phases of enlightenment by Buddhas as numerous as atoms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The causes of the practices and vows of the various vehicles within the six realms— I rejoice in them all and cultivate an ocean of merit;
With a sincere heart, I dedicate these merits,
vowing to study Samantabhadra’s profound faith and understanding, And to perfectly cultivate the myriad practices until they equal the vastness of space.
The reality-limit of Bodhi and all sentient beings— I dedicate them to the profound and tranquil true Dharma-realm.
With a sincere heart,
I make this vow never to abandon the ocean of merit of the thousand wheels, And shall constantly uphold the ten root texts of the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Universally summoning all classes of beings, he opens the sutras as fine as motes of dust; universally gathering all sentient beings, he excises the storehouse of consciousness.
Whether abiding in the state of cause or fruit, he is able to preach the Dharma; whether dwelling among ordinary folk or the sages, he skillfully cultivates the mind.
Within the Universal Eye, one beholds Vairocana; without departing from Samantabhadra, one contemplates Wondrous Virtue.
The three sages are perfectly interfused, returning to the present thought-moment; the ten bodies are unimpeded, responding throughout the realms of dust.
Within the sites of enlightenment across future kalpas and lands, the Dharma King’s eldest son fulfills his equal vows.
I take refuge in the Buddha. May all sentient beings embody and understand the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings penetrate deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings preside over the great assembly, free from all obstacles.
One Scroll of the Liturgy of Praise by the National Teacher Qingliang of Huayan.
